title: Criticism and conflict at work
goal: Give criticism that lands without wounding, receive it without sulking, and help two colleagues make peace — the Indonesian way, where the frame around the message matters as much as the message.
bekal: cushion a criticism with *mohon maaf sebelumnya*, *kurang tepat* and *bukan maksud saya…*
acknowledge the other side before disagreeing: *saya pahami…, namun…*
mediate a quarrel and propose a *jalan tengah* (middle way)

notes: **Punya waktu sepuluh menit?** An Indonesian manager rarely opens with the problem. Asking for a little time, in private, is itself a courtesy: criticism given in front of others costs the listener face, and everyone knows it. Sarah has chosen the small room on purpose.

**Saya pahami kendalanya. Namun, …** — acknowledge first, then turn. *Kendala* (obstacle, constraint) is the polite office word for "problem"; *masalah* sounds heavier. The turn itself comes with *namun*, which in careful writing opens a new sentence.

**Nggak enak** — literally "not pleasant" — is the feeling that stopped Yoga reporting bad news: reluctance to trouble or disappoint a superior. Javanese has a word for this, *ewuh pakewuh*, and every Indonesian office runs on it. A good manager makes it easy to say *ada kendala* early.

**Bukan maksud saya menyalahkan kamu** — "it is not my intention to blame you". Note the order: *bukan maksud saya* first, then the verb. The spoken version is *Aku nggak bermaksud nyalahin kamu*; the Jakarta ending *-in* stands in for standard *-kan*.

**Mohon maaf sebelumnya** — "forgive me in advance" — announces that something unwelcome is coming, which softens it before it arrives. *Kurang tepat* ("less than accurate") is the office way of saying "wrong": *kurang* before an adjective means "not quite", and everybody hears it as "no".

**Siap!** — "ready!" — is the military-flavoured "yes, sir" that has spread into every office, chat group and ojek conversation. *Siap, Mbak* means "understood, I'll do it". 💬 Yoga's *udah*, *bener*, *makasih* and *ngomong* are the everyday forms of *sudah*, *benar*, *terima kasih* and *berbicara*.

grammars.title: The softening ladder
body: Indonesian criticism is rarely wrong in content and almost never blunt in form. Here is the same message climbing from rude to professional.

head: Blunt

Perhaps it could be trimmed a little.

after: Two tools do most of the work: *kurang* + adjective ("not quite X") and the passive, which takes the person out of the sentence. *Laporannya belum masuk* talks about the report; *kamu terlambat* talks about Yoga.
⚠️ Softening is not vagueness. Sarah still names the column, the school and the new deadline. Soft frame, precise content — that is the combination Indonesians respect.

grammars.title: Acknowledge, then turn
body: Before a *but*, Indonesian likes to show that the other person has been heard. These are the standard frames, from formal to casual.

head: Frame
English
Register
rows: It's true that…, it's just that…

after: *Saya pahami* is object-focus: the thing understood can come first, as in *Kendalanya saya pahami*. Both orders are natural.

⚠️ *Namun* is, strictly, a linking word between sentences, so style guides prefer *Saya pahami kendalanya. Namun, …* or *…, tetapi …* inside a single sentence. You will see *…, namun …* everywhere in the press; in your own formal writing, use the full stop.

notes: **Menegur, ditegur, teguran** — to reprimand, to be reprimanded, a reprimand. *Kena tegur* ("hit by a rebuke") is the everyday passive: *kena* marks something unwelcome happening to you, as in *kena macet*, *kena tilang* (get a traffic ticket).

**Iye, aje, kagak** — Fajar's Betawi colours: *iya*, *saja*, *tidak*. Betawi often turns a final *-a* into *-e*: *ape* (apa), *kenape* (kenapa), *aje*. He keeps *saya* with Sarah, his boss, and drops into *gue* the moment he speaks to Yoga man to man.
**Terus terang** — "frankly", literally "straight and clear". Indonesians use it to flag that directness is coming, much as English uses "to be honest". Its formal cousin is *sejujurnya*.
**Ada benarnya** — "there's some truth in it". *Dua-duanya ada benarnya* (you're both partly right) is the mediator's most useful sentence: nobody wins, nobody loses face.
**Kebawa emosi** is the spoken form of *terbawa emosi*, "carried away by emotion". In Jakarta speech the *ter-* of accident often becomes *ke-*: *kebawa, ketinggalan, kepikiran* (it's on my mind).

**Itung-itung nebus dosa** — *itung-itung* (standard *hitung-hitung*) means "as a way of, you could count it as"; *menebus dosa* is "to atone for a sin". Said with a grin, it turns a humbling moment into a joke, and a joke is how an Indonesian quarrel is usually declared over.

grammars.title: Saying sorry at work: four levels
body: An apology changes shape with the channel and the relationship. Fajar uses the last one, and that is exactly right between colleagues of similar age.

head: Indonesian
Where
English
rows: *Kami mohon maaf atas keterlambatan pengiriman data.*
We apologise for the delay in sending the data.
I apologise, that was my mistake.
Sorry, I'm the one who forgot.
Sorry, mate. I got carried away.

after: *Mohon maaf atas…* (apologise for…) takes a noun, so formal apologies nominalise: *keterlambatan* (lateness), *ketidaknyamanan* (inconvenience), *kesalahan* (error).
To accept, say *Iya, nggak apa-apa* or, more formally, *Tidak apa-apa, sudah saya maafkan*. Refusing an apology outright is very rare; the chill shows instead in silence.

blocks.text: An email that asks for corrections follows a fixed choreography: thanks, a cushion, the facts in the passive, the request, and thanks again. These are the pieces.

If there are any problems, do not hesitate to contact us.

Thank you for your attention and cooperation.

blocks.text: Notice *belum sesuai* ("does not yet match") rather than *tidak sesuai*. *Belum* implies it will be fixed, which is both more hopeful and more polite.

blocks.title: Three things not to do
items: Do not criticise a senior in public, even gently. Ask for *waktu sebentar* and do it in private.
Do not answer criticism with *Tapi…* straight away. Start with *Terima kasih atas masukannya*, then explain.
Do not read silence as agreement. *Iya, Mbak* with no eye contact can mean "I'm hurt and not saying so".
